searches.note: The two shared searches read the 1855 classification and the Rothschild Archive for Lafite and Mouton together. One Mouton search was refused for a blocked domain and is counted. Eight of the Haut-Brion and Mouton searches went on people's dates, which result summaries often leave out. WebFetch was not tried.

method: The pilot was written with no web search; its sources were marked read: search, but several addresses were never returned by a search here. This recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, strongest claims first: the people and their dates, the classification, the sales, the sites, the grapes, the making and its months, the label words and each beat of the story.

Every source address the pilot listed was tested; where a search never returned it, it was replaced by a page a search did return, so every source in the fragment is one the refuter saw. All are read: search (a result summary, from the estate's own domain where marked primary).

A fact found in two independent sources or one primary stands; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A dead person whose dates were not found in two sources is described rather than named in the story.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches.

tested: The estate's own history: the Ségur family bought the property in the seventeenth century and the planting is credited to Jacques de Ségur; Baron James bought it in August 1868 and died months later; the label as it is known first appeared on the next vintage: confirmed as the estate tells it.

Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur, the Prince of the Vines, 1697 to 1755 in most accounts, who inherited Latour (Wikipedia, Wine Spectator, wein-plus): confirmed; that he was Jacques de Ségur's grandson was not found and is cut.

The court at Versailles: Wine Spectator says Louis XV took to Lafite probably on the advice of the Maréchal de Richelieu, and the estate's journal credits the Duc de Richelieu with its introduction at court; one account calls the story apocryphal. Kept as a legend, the teller described, his dates not found.
The sale of 1784 for debt to a kinsman, Pichard, guillotined on 30 June 1794, and the seizure as national property (wein-plus, Wikipedia, the estate): confirmed.
Lafite first on the 1855 list of first growths (Fine and Rare, Wikipedia's classification page): confirmed.

The auction of 8 August 1868 in Paris, bought by agents for Baron James, against a coalition of Bordeaux merchants (the estate's journal, Wikipedia); Baron James 1792 to 1868, head of the Paris house, died 15 November 1868 (the Rothschild Archive): confirmed.

The making: about fifteen days of fermentation at a controlled temperature and fifteen months in new oak after each barrel is tasted (the estate's page for the grand vin); the estate announced 2025 as the last vintage in its wooden vats: the year and a half is wrong and the vat material is cut.
Carruades: a group of plots adjoining the ridge of the vineyard, which gives the second wine its name (the estate): confirmed; its share of Merlot was not found.
The rules: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British, no dash: sound.

changed.was: Fermented parcel by parcel in wooden and steel vats, then aged for about a year and a half in new oak barrels, many of them made by the estate's own coopers, before it is bottled at the château.
changed.now: Fermented in vats for about a fortnight at a controlled temperature. Each barrel is then tasted on its own before the blend is made, and the wine is aged in new oak barrels for about fifteen months, by the estate's own account, before it is bottled at the château.
changed.why: The estate's own page gives about fifteen days of fermentation and fifteen months in new oak; it has announced 2025 as the last vintage in its wooden vats, so naming the vats would age, and no source tied the grand vin's barrels to its own coopers.

changed.was: Vines were planted at Lafite in the late seventeenth century, most likely by Jacques de Ségur, and his grandson Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur (1697 to 1755), remembered as the Prince of the Vines, built its name in France and abroad; the Maréchal de Richelieu (1696 to 1788) is said to have made it the King's wine at Versailles. Debts forced the Ségurs to sell in 1784, and in the Revolution the estate was seized and sold as national property. When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification for the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1855, Lafite stood first among the four first growths. On 8 August 1868 Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868), head of the family's Paris bank, bought it at auction against a group of Bordeaux merchants who drove the bidding up; he died three months later. The estate took the family's name and carried it through phylloxera, two world wars and the lean years between them. The Carruades plateau beside the vineyard gives its name to the second wine, Carruades de Lafite. For a sommelier, Lafite is the reference for the perfumed, restrained side of Pauillac, the first growth that whispers rather than shouts.
changed.now: Vines were planted at Lafite in the late seventeenth century by the Ségur family, as the estate tells it, and in the eighteenth century Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur (1697 to 1755), who also held Latour, was remembered as the Prince of the Vines. The story goes that the military governor of Guyenne, a friend of the king, made Lafite the wine of the court at Versailles. Heavy debts forced a later Ségur to sell in 1784, to a kinsman who was guillotined in 1794, and the estate was seized and sold as national property. When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification for the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1855, Lafite stood first among the four first growths. On 8 August 1868 Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868), head of the family's Paris bank, bought it at auction in Paris, against a coalition of Bordeaux merchants as the estate tells it, and he died that November, three months later. The estate took the family's name, and the label as it is known first appeared on the next vintage. The Carruades plateau that adjoins the vineyard gives its name to the second wine. For a sommelier, Lafite is the perfumed, restrained side of Pauillac, the first growth that whispers rather than shouts.
changed.why: Jacques de Ségur's dates were found nowhere and the grandson was not confirmed; the Maréchal de Richelieu's dates were not found in two sources, so the teller of the legend is described; the kinsman of 1784, the Paris auction, the coalition of merchants, the death in November and the label of the next vintage were found; the line on phylloxera and the wars rested on no source.

changed.was: A fortified tower stood here in the fourteenth century, guarding the estuary during the Hundred Years War, and it gave the estate its name; the round tower that stands there now, and on every label, was built later. By the early eighteenth century Latour had joined Lafite in the hands of the Ségur family, and in 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked it among the four first growths. The Ségur heirs kept it until 1963, when they sold a majority to the British Pearson group, with Harveys of Bristol beside it. The new owners rebuilt the cellar and in 1964 replaced the old wooden vats with temperature controlled stainless steel, three years after Haut-Brion and well ahead of most of Bordeaux. Les Forts de Latour, the second wine, followed with the 1966 vintage, and the estate returned to French hands in 1993. Latour is famous for consistency: its deep gravel by the river gives a wine that holds its shape in weak years, and its 1961 is a vintage of history. With the 2012 vintage it left the en primeur system, the sale of wine still in barrel, and has since released its wines when it judges them ready to drink.

changed.was: The estate was shaped in the sixteenth century by the Lestonnac family, who turned a medieval domain called La Mothe towards wine. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), then the American minister in Paris, toured Bordeaux and named Château Margaux among four wines of the first quality, with Latour, Haut-Brion and Lafite. After the Revolution the Marquis de la Colonilla bought the estate in the early nineteenth century and had the architect Louis Combes build the neoclassical château, begun in 1810, that appears on the label. In 1855 the brokers ranked Château Margaux a first growth, one of only four reds. The twentieth century brought hard times: the Ginestet family, Bordeaux merchants, held it through lean decades and sold it in 1977 to André Mentzelopoulos (1915 to 1980), who restored the vineyards and cellars before his death, with the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) as adviser. The run of vintages from 1978 onwards brought the estate's name back. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is all Sauvignon Blanc, and since the Margaux appellation is for red wine alone it must be sold as Bordeaux Blanc.
changed.now: In the 1570s the Lestonnac family reshaped the old domain at Margaux around its vineyards, as the estate tells it. In 1787 Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826), then the American minister in Paris, toured Bordeaux and named Château Margaux among four wines of the first quality, with Latour, Haut-Brion and Lafite. After the Revolution the estate was sold as national property, and its new owner of 1801 had a Bordeaux architect build the neoclassical château, begun in 1810, whose front appears on the label. In 1855 the brokers ranked Château Margaux a first growth, one of only four reds. The twentieth century was harder: the Ginestet family, who had come to own the whole estate by about 1950, were left in difficulty by the slump of the 1970s and sold it in 1977 to André Mentzelopoulos (1915 to 1980). He drained and replanted the vineyard, with the oenologist Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004) as adviser, and by his death in 1980 the estate was held to have its old standing back. Its white, Pavillon Blanc, is all Sauvignon Blanc, and since the Margaux appellation is for red wine alone it must be sold as Bordeaux Blanc.
changed.why: The estate's own history gives the Lestonnac decade, 1801, 1810, the Ginestets' whole estate by about 1950, the slump and the sale of 1977; the buyer of 1801 and the architect have no dates in two sources; Mentzelopoulos is dated by the estate and French Wikipedia; Wikipedia, not the run of 1978, is the source for the estate's standing restored by 1980.

changed.was: Jean de Pontac married into the Haut-Brion lands in 1525 and acquired the estate in 1533, and his descendants made it one of the first Bordeaux wines sold under the name of its own estate. Arnaud III de Pontac (1599 to 1681) sold it in London, and on 10 April 1663 Samuel Pepys (1633 to 1703) wrote in his diary of drinking a French wine called Ho Bryan, an early written note on a Bordeaux estate. Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826) visited in 1787 and bought its wine, and the statesman Talleyrand (1754 to 1838) owned it briefly in the early nineteenth century. In 1855 the brokers could not leave it out: it was ranked a first growth beside three Médoc estates, though it lies in the Graves. The American banker Clarence Dillon (1882 to 1979) bought it in 1935. In 1959 it was classified again, among the red Crus Classés de Graves, and in 1961 it became the first of the first growths to ferment in stainless steel vats. Its white, Haut-Brion Blanc, is one of the few dry white wines of Bordeaux to stand beside the reds.
changed.now: In 1525 a marriage brought part of the Haut-Brion land to the Pontac family as a bride's dowry; in 1533 the bridegroom bought its manorial rights from a Basque merchant, and in 1549 he began the château. By the 1660s the wine was known in London by the estate's own name: on 10 April 1663 Samuel Pepys (1633 to 1703) wrote in his diary of drinking, at the Royal Oak tavern in Lombard Street, a French wine called Ho Bryan, and in 1666 the family opened a London tavern of its own, Pontack's Head. Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826) came on 25 May 1787 and bought its wine, and the statesman Talleyrand (1754 to 1838) owned it briefly in the early nineteenth century. In 1855 the brokers ranked it a first growth beside three Médoc estates, though it lies in the Graves. In 1935 a New York banker bought it, and the second wine, Le Clarence, carries his first name. In 1959 it was classified again, among the red Crus Classés de Graves, and in 1961 it became the first of the first growths to ferment in stainless steel vats. Its white, Haut-Brion Blanc, carries no classification of its own.
changed.why: The estate's own history gives every date of the Pontacs and of Jefferson's visit; Arnaud III's dates conflict and Jean de Pontac's were not found, so neither is named; Pepys's tavern is the diary's; the banker of 1935 is dated by Wikipedia alone, so he is described; the white's lack of a classification is the library's; the brokers' motive and the white's standing were judgements no source gave.

changed.was: Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild (1812 to 1870), of the English branch of the family, bought Château Brane-Mouton in 1853 and gave it his family's name. Two years later the brokers' classification of 1855 placed it at the head of the second growths, a slight the family never accepted. His great grandson, Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), took charge in 1922 and changed Bordeaux: from the 1924 vintage he bottled the whole crop at the château, when most estates sold their wine in cask to merchants, and that year's label was drawn by the poster artist Jean Carlu (1900 to 1997). In 1945 he marked the Liberation with a label bearing a V for victory by Philippe Jullian (1919 to 1977), and since then a different artist has made part of each year's label. The old motto ran: first I cannot be, second I do not deign, Mouton I am. After decades of campaigning, a decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, and the motto became: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change. In 1979 Philippe de Rothschild founded Opus One in Napa with Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008).
changed.now: Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild (1812 to 1870), of the English branch of the family, bought Château Brane-Mouton in 1853, and the estate took the family's name. Two years later the brokers' classification of 1855 placed it among the second growths, a rank the family would not accept. His great grandson, Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), took charge in 1922, barely twenty, and from the 1924 vintage bottled the whole crop at the château, where until then the wine had been sold in barrel to the Bordeaux merchants; that year's label was drawn by a young poster artist in the Cubist manner. In 1945 he marked the year of victory with a label bearing a V for victory, by a then unknown illustrator, and since then a different artist has made the work at the head of each year's label. The old motto ran: first I cannot be, second I do not deign, Mouton I am. After some twenty years of campaigning, a decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, and the motto became: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change. In 1978 Philippe de Rothschild agreed with a Napa winemaker to make one wine together, Opus One, first made from the 1979 vintage.
changed.why: Among the second growths, not at their head; Philippe's age and the sale in barrel are the estate's; the artists of 1924 and 1945 and the Napa partner have no dates in two sources; Opus One was agreed in 1978 and first made in 1979; changed Bordeaux was a judgement.
